lessons.title: Delivering Products by Bicycle, Motorbike, or Pickup
lessons.body:
When you start selling tissues and paper products, you need a reliable way to get them to your customers. The three most common delivery vehicles in African cities and towns are bicycles, motorbikes, and pickups. Each has its place. A bicycle is cheap to buy and maintain, needs no fuel, and can carry up to 30 kg if you use a rear rack and saddlebags. Use it for short distances under 5 km and small orders like 10 to 20 tissue packs. A motorbike costs more but moves faster and can carry up to 80 kg with a strong rear box. It is ideal for 5â15 km deliveries and medium orders. A pickup truck is for bulk orders â 200 kg or more â and can cover 20â50 km. You can hire one when needed instead of buying.

Before you load, always check the weather. Paper products are ruined by rain. Invest in a waterproof tarpaulin or large plastic bags. For bicycles, use a covered basket or panniers. For motorbikes, a lockable top box keeps goods dry and secure. For pickups, tie down the load with ropes and cover with a tarp. Never stack heavy items on top of soft tissue rolls â they will crush and become unsellable.

Plan your delivery route to avoid backtracking. If you have 10 customers, group them by area. Deliver to the furthest point first, then work your way back. This saves fuel and time. For a motorbike, a full tank of 5 litres costs about 5,000â7,000 shillings (or equivalent) and can cover 150 km. Charge delivery fees that cover your costs: for a 5 km bicycle delivery, charge 1,000 shillings; for a 10 km motorbike delivery, charge 2,500 shillings; for a pickup, charge 10,000 shillings plus fuel.

Maintain your vehicle. For bicycles, check tyre pressure weekly and oil the chain monthly. For motorbikes, change engine oil every 1,500 km and check brakes. For pickups, service every 5,000 km. A breakdown means lost sales and spoiled goods. Keep a basic tool kit: spanner, tyre pump, patch kit, and spare inner tube. Always carry a phone with mobile money and a contact number for a local mechanic. With good planning and care, your delivery vehicle becomes a money-making asset, not a headache.

lessons.title: Working with Local Transporters for Bulk Orders
lessons.body:
When you land a big order â say 500 tissue packs for a hotel or 1,000 rolls for a supermarket â your bicycle or motorbike won't cut it. You need a local transporter. These are individuals or small companies with pickups, lorries, or tuk-tuks who move goods for a fee. They are found at markets, transport stages, or through word of mouth. Building good relationships with them is key to growing your business.

Start by identifying 3â4 reliable transporters in your area. Ask other shop owners who they use. When you meet a transporter, agree on clear terms: price per trip, loading and offloading help, and time of delivery. For a 1-tonne pickup within 20 km, expect to pay 30,000â50,000 shillings. For a 3-tonne lorry within 50 km, 100,000â150,000 shillings. Always negotiate, but don't squeeze too hard â a fair price ensures they handle your goods with care. Get a written agreement or at least a WhatsApp message confirming the deal, including date, time, and price.

Before loading, inspect the truck: is it clean, dry, and free of sharp edges? Paper products absorb moisture and smells. If the truck previously carried fish or cement, insist on a clean tarpaulin lining. Load boxes neatly, with heavier ones at the bottom. Use straps to secure the load. Count every box with the transporter present and note the number on the delivery note. Both of you sign. This prevents disputes later.

During transit, stay in touch. Call the driver halfway to confirm progress. If you are not travelling with the goods, ensure the receiver knows the expected arrival time and has your number. On arrival, the receiver should count and inspect the goods before signing. Any damage or shortage must be noted on the delivery note immediately. Take photos as evidence.

Pay the transporter promptly after delivery is confirmed. A happy transporter will prioritise your future orders, offer discounts, and even help you find backhaul loads to reduce costs. Treat them as partners, not just service providers. Over time, you can negotiate a monthly contract for regular deliveries, which saves money and guarantees availability.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Simple Distribution Route
lessons.body:
A distribution route is simply a plan for where you will deliver and in what order. Without a route, you waste fuel, time, and energy. With a good route, you can serve more customers in less time and make more profit. Start by listing all your customers â shops, hotels, schools, market stalls â and mark them on a map or a hand-drawn sketch. Group them by area: for example, 'Market Road', 'Town Centre', 'Industrial Area'.

Next, decide how often you will visit each area. If you have many customers in one area, visit that area on a fixed day each week. For example, Monday: Market Road; Tuesday: Town Centre; Wednesday: Industrial Area; Thursday: repeat Market Road; Friday: new customer hunting. This schedule lets customers know when to expect you, so they can prepare their orders and cash. It also reduces your travel distance because you cover one area at a time.

For each route, plan the order of stops to avoid crossing back and forth. Start with the furthest stop, then work back towards your base. Use a notebook or a simple app like Google Maps to estimate distances. If you use a motorbike, aim for no more than 40 km per day. For a bicycle, 15 km. For a pickup, 80 km. Calculate your fuel or energy cost and set a minimum order size per stop â for example, 5 packs of tissues â to make the trip worthwhile.

Keep a delivery log. Each day, record: customer name, items delivered, amount collected, and any issues. This log helps you track which customers are growing, which are not paying, and which areas need more attention. After one month, review your routes. Are some stops too far for the profit? Can you combine two small stops into one? Adjust as needed.

Finally, always have a backup plan. If a road is flooded or a customer is closed, move to the next stop and come back later. Inform the customer via call or SMS. A reliable route builds trust and turns one-time buyers into regular customers. Start simple, be consistent, and refine over time.

lessons.title: Managing Cash on Delivery and Mobile Money Payments
lessons.body:
Most small tissue and paper product sales in Africa are cash on delivery (COD) or mobile money. COD means the customer pays when you hand over the goods. Mobile money means they send money via M-Pesa, Airtel Money, MTN MoMo, or similar. Both have risks: fake notes, robbery, and failed transfers. You need simple systems to protect your money.

For COD, always carry a small cash box or a locked bag. Never flash large amounts of cash. If a customer pays with a large note, count the change carefully in front of them. Use a calculator or your phone to confirm totals. For amounts over 50,000 shillings, ask for mobile money instead. If you must accept cash, meet in a safe place â a shop, not a dark street. After each delivery, record the amount received in your log and reconcile at the end of the day. Deposit cash into your bank or mobile money account the same day or next morning. Don't keep it at home.

For mobile money, always confirm the payment before releasing goods. Ask the customer to show you the confirmation SMS or the transaction ID. Call your own phone to check the balance if needed. Beware of fake SMS screenshots â they are common. The safest method is to dial your mobile money balance code (e.g., *144# for M-Pesa) and verify the money is in your account. If the network is down, ask the customer to pay cash or reschedule delivery. Never accept a promise to pay later unless you know the customer well and have a signed credit agreement.

Set clear payment terms. For regular customers, you might allow payment within 7 days, but only if they have a history of paying on time. For new customers, insist on COD or mobile money upfront. Keep a record of every transaction: date, customer, items, amount, payment method, and balance (if any). Use a simple notebook or a free app like Wave or Keeper. At the end of each week, total your sales and compare with cash and mobile money received. Any shortage means you need to tighten your process.

Train anyone who delivers for you. They must follow the same rules: no goods without payment, no cash kept overnight, and always verify mobile money. A small mistake can wipe out your profit for the day. Be firm but polite. Most customers respect a business that is organised and secure.

lessons.title: Storing Finished Goods to Avoid Moisture and Pests
lessons.body:
Tissues and paper products are like sponges â they absorb moisture from the air. Damp paper grows mould, smells bad, and loses strength. Pests like rats, cockroaches, and silverfish also love to chew and nest in paper. Proper storage is not optional; it is the difference between selling at full price and throwing away stock. You don't need a fancy warehouse. A dry, clean room with good airflow works.

First, choose the right room. It should be above ground level, with no leaks, and away from kitchens, bathrooms, or washing areas. If you store in a shop, keep goods on shelves at least 30 cm off the floor and 10 cm away from walls. This allows air to circulate and prevents moisture from seeping in. Use wooden pallets or plastic crates to raise boxes. Never stack boxes directly on a damp floor or against a cold wall.

Control moisture. If your area is humid or rainy, use cheap desiccants like silica gel packets (save them from new shoe boxes or buy in bulk) or charcoal in open containers. Place them near the stock. You can also run a fan for an hour a day to keep air moving. If you have electricity, a dehumidifier is excellent but expensive. A simple hygrometer (costs about 10,000 shillings) tells you the humidity level. Keep it below 60%. If it rises, open windows on dry days or use a fan.

Prevent pests. Keep the room clean â no food crumbs, no old cardboard lying around. Seal cracks and holes with cement or steel wool. Use traps, not poison, near paper goods. Cats are good for rats but may tear paper, so avoid them in the storage room. Inspect your stock weekly. Look for tiny holes, droppings, or a musty smell. If you find pests, isolate the affected boxes and treat the room with a safe insecticide (follow instructions) or call a pest control service. For small infestations, you can freeze paper products for 48 hours to kill eggs and larvae â but only if you have a large freezer and the goods are sealed in plastic.

Rotate your stock. Use the 'first in, first out' (FIFO) method. Older boxes go out first. Write the date received on each box with a marker. Never store goods for more than 3 months if you can help it. Check your stock weekly for any signs of damage. A little effort in storage saves you from big losses. Remember: dry, clean, and pest-free means your tissues stay soft and sellable.

lessons.title: Handling Returns and Damaged Goods Professionally
lessons.body:
Even with the best care, some goods will be returned or damaged. A customer might complain that tissues are torn, wet, or the wrong type. A box might fall off a truck. How you handle these situations determines whether you keep that customer and your reputation. The rule is simple: be professional, be fair, and follow a clear process.

First, listen to the customer. Let them explain the problem without interrupting. Thank them for bringing it to your attention. If the return is due to your error â wrong item, damaged in transit, or expired â you must make it right. Offer a replacement or a refund, whichever the customer prefers. If the damage is minor (e.g., a few crushed rolls in a pack), you might offer a discount on their next order instead. But never argue or blame the customer in public. That destroys trust.

For damaged goods, inspect them immediately. Take photos. If the damage happened during delivery, note it on the delivery note and inform your transporter. If you have insurance or a good relationship with the transporter, you may recover part of the cost. If the damage is due to poor storage, learn from it and improve. Separate damaged goods from good stock. Do not try to sell damaged tissues at full price â it will backfire. You can sell them at a discount to a local market or use them for cleaning rags, but be honest about the condition.

Create a simple returns policy. Write it down and share it with regular customers. For example: 'Returns accepted within 3 days for damaged or wrong items. Goods must be in original packaging. Refund or replacement within 7 days.' This sets expectations and reduces disputes. For cash refunds, get a signed receipt from the customer. For replacements, record the exchange in your log.

Track returns. If a particular product keeps getting returned, stop buying it. If a particular customer returns items too often, have a polite conversation. Maybe they need a different product or better storage advice. Use returns as feedback to improve your business. A customer who sees you handle a problem well becomes more loyal. A customer who feels cheated tells everyone. Always choose the professional path, even when it costs you a little. In the long run, your reputation is worth more than one box of tissues.

quiz.q: What is the maximum weight a bicycle can typically carry for deliveries if fitted with a rear rack and saddlebags?
quiz.explanation: A bicycle can carry up to 30 kg with proper racks and bags, making it suitable for small orders.

quiz.q: Which delivery vehicle is best for a bulk order of 500 tissue packs over 20 km?
quiz.explanation: A pickup truck can handle bulk orders of 200 kg or more and cover longer distances.

quiz.q: Why should you never stack heavy items on top of soft tissue rolls?
options: A) They will become too heavy to lift
B) They will crush and become unsellable
quiz.explanation: Heavy items crush soft tissue rolls, damaging them and making them unsellable.

quiz.q: What is a good way to protect paper products from rain during bicycle delivery?
options: A) Wrap them in a cotton cloth
B) Use a waterproof tarpaulin or large plastic bags
C) Leave them uncovered for quick drying
D) Stack them on top of the bicycle
quiz.explanation: Waterproof tarpaulins or plastic bags keep paper products dry during rain.

quiz.q: How much might you charge for a 5 km bicycle delivery to cover your costs?
quiz.explanation: A typical charge for a 5 km bicycle delivery is around 1,000 shillings to cover time and effort.

quiz.q: What is a key maintenance task for a motorbike used for deliveries?
options: A) Change engine oil every 1,500 km
B) Replace the seat every month
C) Paint the fuel tank weekly
D) Remove the rear box daily
quiz.explanation: Regular oil changes every 1,500 km keep the motorbike engine running reliably.

quiz.q: When hiring a local transporter for a 1-tonne pickup within 20 km, what is a reasonable price range?
quiz.explanation: A 1-tonne pickup within 20 km typically costs between 30,000 and 50,000 shillings.

quiz.q: Why should you inspect a transporter's truck before loading paper products?
options: B) To ensure it is clean, dry, and free of sharp edges
C) To see if it has a radio
D) To check the tyre brand
quiz.explanation: Paper products absorb moisture and smells, so the truck must be clean and dry to prevent damage.

quiz.q: What should you do if a transporter's truck previously carried fish?
options: A) Refuse to use the truck
B) Insist on a clean tarpaulin lining
C) Spray perfume in the truck
D) Load quickly to avoid smell
quiz.explanation: A clean tarpaulin lining prevents fish odours from contaminating paper products.

quiz.q: During transit of bulk goods, what is a good practice to prevent disputes?
options: A) Count every box with the transporter present and both sign
B) Trust the transporter to count alone
C) Only count if you suspect theft
D) Skip counting to save time
quiz.explanation: Counting together and signing a delivery note prevents later disagreements over shortages.

quiz.q: How can you reduce transport costs for regular bulk deliveries?
options: A) Negotiate a monthly contract with a transporter
B) Always use the most expensive transporter
quiz.explanation: A monthly contract can secure lower rates and guaranteed availability.

quiz.q: What is the first step in setting up a simple distribution route?
options: B) List all customers and mark them on a map
quiz.explanation: Listing and mapping customers helps group them by area for efficient routing.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to visit the same area on a fixed day each week?
options: A) Customers know when to expect you and can prepare orders
C) It allows you to sleep late
D) It reduces the number of customers
quiz.explanation: A fixed schedule helps customers prepare and builds trust, while reducing travel distance.

quiz.q: What is a recommended maximum daily distance for a motorbike delivery route?
quiz.explanation: Aim for no more than 40 km per day on a motorbike to manage fuel and time efficiently.

quiz.q: What is a 'delivery log' used for?
options: A) To record customer names, items, amounts, and issues
B) To track your vehicle's fuel consumption only
quiz.explanation: A delivery log tracks sales, payments, and problems, helping you manage and improve routes.

quiz.q: What does COD stand for in delivery?
quiz.explanation: COD means the customer pays in cash when the goods are delivered.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid accepting large cash notes for payment?
options: B) They increase risk of fake notes and robbery
C) They are not accepted by banks
D) They take longer to count
quiz.explanation: Large notes are more likely to be counterfeit and attract robbers, so mobile money is safer.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to confirm a mobile money payment before releasing goods?
options: B) Dial your mobile money balance code and verify
C) Ask the customer to swear
D) Accept a promise to pay later
quiz.explanation: Dialling your balance code confirms the money is actually in your account, avoiding fake screenshots.

quiz.q: What should you do if the mobile money network is down during a delivery?
options: A) Release goods and hope for payment later
B) Ask for cash or reschedule delivery
D) Give a discount for the inconvenience
quiz.explanation: If network is down, request cash or reschedule to avoid non-payment.

quiz.q: How often should you reconcile your cash and mobile money records?
options: B) At the end of each week
quiz.explanation: Weekly reconciliation helps you spot shortages and tighten your payment process.

quiz.q: Why should you store paper products on shelves at least 30 cm off the floor?
options: A) To make them look nice
B) To allow air circulation and prevent moisture
C) To make them harder to steal
quiz.explanation: Raising goods off the floor allows air to circulate and prevents moisture from seeping in.

quiz.q: What is a cheap way to control humidity in a storage room?
options: A) Use silica gel packets or charcoal
B) Spray water in the air
D) Store goods in the bathroom
quiz.explanation: Silica gel and charcoal absorb moisture and are inexpensive desiccants.

quiz.q: What humidity level should you aim for to keep paper products dry?
quiz.explanation: Keeping humidity below 60% prevents mould and moisture damage.

quiz.q: What is the FIFO method for stock rotation?
quiz.explanation: FIFO means older stock is sold first to prevent spoilage and expiry.

quiz.q: How can you kill pest eggs and larvae in paper products without chemicals?
options: C) Expose them to sunlight for a week
quiz.explanation: Freezing sealed paper products for 48 hours kills eggs and larvae.

quiz.q: What should you do first when a customer returns a product?
options: A) Listen to the customer without interrupting
quiz.explanation: Listening calmly shows respect and helps you understand the issue before responding.

quiz.q: If the return is due to your error, what should you offer?
options: C) A discount on future orders only
D) A free gift unrelated to the product
quiz.explanation: You must make it right by offering a replacement or refund for your mistake.

quiz.q: What should you do with damaged goods that cannot be sold at full price?
options: A) Sell them at a discount honestly
B) Hide the damage and sell at full price
C) Throw them away without trying
quiz.explanation: Selling damaged goods at a discount is honest and recovers some value.

quiz.q: Why is a written returns policy useful?
options: A) It sets clear expectations and reduces disputes
C) It is required by law in all countries
D) It allows you to refuse all returns
quiz.explanation: A written policy clarifies terms for both you and the customer, minimising disagreements.

quiz.q: What should you do if a particular product keeps getting returned?
quiz.explanation: Frequent returns indicate a quality issue, so discontinue that product.
